name: Colonialism
summary: Colonialism is the rule of a territory and its people by a foreign state, which holds political and economic control for its own advantage. In its classical European defence (c. 1870-1930) it combined a claimed civilising duty or trusteeship over peoples seen as less advanced with arguments about markets, raw materials, naval power and national standing. Adherents accepted hierarchy between peoples, strong executive authority, force to keep the territory, and gradual preparation for self-rule at most.
scope: The mainstream metropolitan justification of European overseas empire in the high imperial era, based on Jules Ferry's 1884-85 case for French expansion and Frederick Lugard's The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922), read with the reference and scholarly treatments of colonialism. It excludes anticolonial and postcolonial critics, and earlier mercantile or Iberian conquest-era views except where the reference article describes them; settler, exploitation and national colonialism are treated as one family, so answers on settlement are partly inferred.

sources.title: Colonialism
sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: Philosophical justifications (Mill, Vitoria, civilising mission), the critics (Marx, Lenin, Said, Fanon) and liberal imperial administration.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Colonial administrations provided limited health and sanitation services to serve rule and trade, not as a universal state guarantee to subjects; inferred from Lugard's trusteeship framing of welfare as paternal, not a right.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Colonial economies depended on cheap native labour; Lugard wants labour free of unpaid exactions but sees wages set by local conditions and trade, so a large statutory rise is not part of the programme.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Ferry and Lugard want trade and private enterprise opening new markets and raw materials, though the colonial state and chartered companies directed it heavily; mercantilist rather than laissez-faire.

public-ownership.rationale: Colonial economies ran largely through chartered and private companies, with the state building railways and ports where needed; public ownership of major industries was not a doctrine.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Lugard's tax discussion concerns hut and poll taxes on colonial subjects to fund administration; soaking wealthy settlers and firms was not a colonial aim.

unions-good.rationale: Colonial authorities generally restricted or suppressed native labour organisation; inferred from the exploitation-colonialism pattern described in the reference article.

property-fundamental.rationale: Lugard treats land tenure and property as things the suzerain regulates and may reserve, so property is respected for settlers and firms but not beyond the colonial state's power.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Ferry wants firms and markets expanded abroad with state backing; tight regulation of the commercial interests that colonies serve is not part of the case.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare is not a theme of colonial doctrine; imperial rule and metropolitan social policy varied by country and era.

worker-ownership.rationale: Colonies served metropolitan owners and companies; collective worker ownership runs against the economic purpose of extracting resources and markets for the metropole.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Colonial states policed subjects heavily to keep order, so security measures were readily accepted; terrorism per se is anachronistic, hence inferred.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Colonial states often taxed and monopolised opium and alcohol for revenue yet cast themselves as moral guardians; no consistent legalisation stance, mild lean to control.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Colonial rulers restricted native political speech and press, but not to protect subjects from insult; inferred hostile to such rules.

strong-leader.rationale: Lugard's model puts a Governor with wide powers over chiefs and subjects, and Ferry demands decisive state action abroad, so executive vigour over gridlock fits.

state-harmful.rationale: Lugard states that the suzerain alone holds the right to impose taxation and confirms or deposes native rulers; colonialism is a doctrine of strong state authority.

limit-guns.rationale: Lugard bars native rulers from raising armed forces, and colonial states typically disarmed subjects, though settlers kept arms; inferred.

empower-police-military.rationale: Ferry grounds expansion in naval and military needs, and colonial rule rested on force and constabulary; adherents back stronger armed forces.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Colonial regimes both regulated brothels for soldiers and enforced moral campaigns; adherents were split, so neutral.

decide-locally.rationale: Lugard's indirect rule lets chiefs administer locally under British supervision and a single government, yet final authority stays with the colonial state; decentralisation is administrative only.

rehabilitation.rationale: Colonial penal systems leaned on punishment, flogging and forced labour; rehabilitation is inferred as secondary.

traditional-family.rationale: Lugard wants institutions rooted in native custom, and metropolitan colonial ideology prized the conventional family and missions' moral reform; mild support.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Colonial powers criminalised homosexuality in many colonies and held conventional Christian morality; adherents would reject legal same-sex marriage.

abortion-legal.rationale: Christian missions and colonial law restricted abortion, and pronatalism served settlement and labour supply; adherents lean against.

more-religion-public.rationale: The civilising mission was often rooted in Christian mission, and colonial states supported missions and religion in schooling; mildly supportive.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Ferry's claim that superior races have a duty to rule the inferior presupposes racial hierarchy, so adherents would deny a duty to correct historical racial injustices.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Colonial ideology assumed fixed natural differences among peoples and sexes; the social-construct thesis is a later critical view, so mild disagree inferred.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Ferry ties colonial expansion to national greatness and a first-rank France, which implies strong attachment to the home nation's culture and standing.

gradual-change.rationale: Lugard warns that going too fast risks more disappointment than going too slowly and says complete independence is not yet on the horizon, and he builds on chiefs' existing institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Colonial powers encouraged settler emigration outward and in places imported labour; reducing migration to the metropole was not a stated aim, so mild disagree, inferred.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Ferry holds that nations stay great by acting for themselves and warns against abstention; supranational authority over empire is not part of the case, though the League mandates later used trusteeship language.

free-trade.rationale: Ferry cites protectionist rivals to justify securing exclusive colonial markets, while Lugard holds that open trade in African produce benefits all; colonial thinkers were split between preference and open door.

nation-first.rationale: Ferry argues that France must act for its own interest and naval and commercial needs, warning that abstention would drop it from the first rank to the third or fourth.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Ferry presents civilising and ending slavery and barbarism as a duty of the higher races, an ancestor of intervention for human rights, though framed by hierarchy.

open-borders.rationale: Colonialism is control of territory and population by a foreign state with legally unequal subjects; open borders contradict that control and the settler and subject statuses it created.

limit-growth.rationale: Colonial expansion aimed at growing markets, resources and industry, as Ferry's argument on export outlets shows; limiting growth for the environment is opposed.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Climate change was not an issue for colonial ideology; its emphasis on extraction and development implies no support for drastic action.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Lugard holds that Europe's technology, railways and trade develop African resources and uplift people, and the civilising mission relied on belief in progress through European science.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Nuclear power postdates the classical colonial period; neither support nor opposition follows from its principles.

revolution-justified.rationale: Colonial rule treated anticolonial rebellion as something to suppress, as the reference article notes, and its adherents defend order and legitimate authority.

experts-over-public.rationale: Mill's liberal imperial model, as SEP describes it, rests on an appointed administrative corps with local knowledge not accountable to the governed, and Lugard relies on trained officers.

central-planning.rationale: Colonial economies were directed by metropolitan interest through mercantilist rules and chartered companies, but not by central planning of the whole economy; mild disagree.

socialized-markets.rationale: Colonial trade ran through private and chartered companies for metropolitan profit; worker or public ownership of firms is inferred as foreign to it.

land-value-tax.rationale: Lugard describes hut and poll taxes on subjects and state control of land, not a land-value tax replacing others; inferred from his tax discussion.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Colonial elites and settlers were propertied beneficiaries of empire and no source ties the doctrine to heavy inheritance taxation.

basic-income.rationale: Lugard emphasises free labour and initiative as the engine of prosperity and taxes subjects; an unconditional state payment cuts against that.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Ferry cites German and American protectionism as the reason France needs colonial outlets, and mercantilist empires used tariffs to bind colonies to the metropole.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The reference article describes colonial rule via mercantilism and chartered companies, with the state steering colonial investment toward ports, railways and extraction.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Settler colonialism and plantations concentrated land in settler and company hands, and exploitation colonies relied on estates; widespread smallholding is not its aim.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Colonial rule turned on taxation and wage or cash-crop labour to draw subjects into the metropole's economy, and the reference article places it within mercantile trade; abolition of money is opposed.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Colonial currencies were typically issued by metropole-controlled bodies; abolition is not part of the doctrine, inferred.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Not addressed; colonial states sometimes controlled labour through official bodies but no consistent doctrine exists.

one-party-rule.rationale: Colonial rule was by a foreign administration, not a single ideological party; metropoles were mostly parliamentary, so mild disagree.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Lugard works through hereditary emirs and chiefs, and many empires were crowned, so hereditary monarchy is an accepted form.

democracy-best.rationale: Lugard argues that representative government based on an educated minority is unsuited to African tribes, and Mill defended despotism for backward peoples; democracy is not held best for subjects.

direct-votes.rationale: Lugard rejects popular representation for colonial subjects and holds that rule is by trained officials with chiefs; direct votes on laws run against that.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils as the basis of political power contradict foreign control; colonial rule monopolised power in the hands of the colonial state.

right-to-secede.rationale: Ferry says France shall never leave its overseas territories, and Lugard says the era of independence is not visible; a right to secede is denied.

natural-rulers.rationale: Ferry asserts that the superior races have a right to rule the inferior, and Lugard speaks of ruling castes more capable of rule; natural fitness to rule is assumed.

political-violence-never.rationale: Conquest, pacification and suppression of rebellion were integral to colonial rule, so adherents do not hold political violence is never justified.

war-builds-character.rationale: Ferry links imperial power to national greatness and martial strength; adherents often prized martial virtue, but this is inferred rather than stated.

separate-church-state.rationale: Colonial rule was frequently allied with missions as part of the civilising mission, though some regimes such as French republican ones were secular; mild lean against strict separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Lugard keeps native custom and sharia in emirates under British supervision but metropolitan law remained supreme; scripture as the basis of law is not the doctrine.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Lugard reserves force, taxation and justice to the suzerain power; private provision of courts and defence is excluded.

military-superiority.rationale: Ferry argues France needs coaling stations and secure ports, saying a ship without coal is a wreck, to preserve naval standing among great powers; superiority is central.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The reference article distinguishes settler, exploitation and national colonialism; adherents differed on ethnic purity of the nation, so neutral.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Lugard describes reciprocal benefit between rulers, trade and native peoples, not class conflict as history's engine; Marxist views appear only as critics in the SEP.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The civilising-mission doctrine assumes a hierarchy of peoples and unequal standing; equal outcomes is rejected.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Lugard states that native rulers cannot appropriate land and the suzerain holds the sole right of taxation and ultimate control; Indigenous authority over land is denied.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Lugard defends British rule as a benefit with reciprocal gains and answers critics who call it exploitation, so owing reparations is rejected.

civilizational-union.rationale: Colonial powers competed with one another, and shared religion or civilisation did not produce political union; mild disagree, inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Ferry's case for expansion rests on national economic interest, but it is clothed in duty; individual self-interest as virtue is weakly implied.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Ferry frames the right of superior races as flowing from a duty, and colonial doctrine was paternalist, putting duty ahead of subjects' rights.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Lugard defends developing wild resources such as oil-nuts that otherwise rotted; nature is valued for use.

limit-population.rationale: Colonial settlers and rulers valued population for labour and settlement; active limitation is not documented as policy.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Lugard praises European industry and trade as developing Africa's resources for the world; industrial civilisation as a disaster is the opposite view.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Lugard praises technology but also urges slow institutional change; disruptive acceleration is not endorsed.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic for classical colonialism; no positions documented, though some racial-improvement ideas existed.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic; Lugard's trained administrator model would reject handing decisions to algorithms, inferred.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Colonial states sought to control communications and reserved security power to the suzerain; inferred.

restore-past-order.rationale: Lugard preserves native custom through indirect rule but promotes progress toward development; adherents split between order and progress.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Lugard defends British rule with trade figures and practical outcomes, and Ferry argues from needs; a pragmatic tone fits.

direct-action.rationale: Colonial authorities suppressed anticolonial movements that used direct action; adherents prefer order through the state.

means-match-ends.rationale: Colonial rule used coercion to promote civilisation and prosperity, so means are not expected to mirror the ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Lugard condemns waste of unexploited resources and the civilising mission aims at settled agriculture and trade; foraging is the antithesis.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The colonial economy depended on specialised labour producing export crops and minerals; abolition of the division of labour is opposed.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Lugard's colonial economy rests on trade, taxation and reward for labour; distribution by need is a socialist aim outside it.

production-for-use.rationale: Ferry argues that colonies are needed as outlets for industry and commerce, a profit-driven rationale, so production for need rather than profit is rejected.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Lugard defends profits from trade and resource development as reciprocal and widely shared; the claim that profit equals exploitation is the Marxist critique he answers.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The SEP presents Marx and Lenin as critics of empire; colonial adherents oppose working-class dictatorship strongly.

collective-farming.rationale: Colonial agriculture used plantations, estates, settler farms and peasant cash crops; collective farming is a communist policy foreign to it.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The SEP records Lenin's and others' claim that imperial competition arose from monopoly capital; adherents of colonialism deny it and defend empire.

taxation-theft.rationale: Lugard says the sole right to impose taxation is reserved to the suzerain power and that tax replaces tribute and forced labour; taxation is legitimate.

harm-principle.rationale: Mill, the harm principle's author, held that despotic rule over backward peoples is legitimate as a means to improvement, so adherents do not confine state restriction to preventing harm.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Lugard's system recognises tribes, chiefs and native custom as units of rule, and subjects held unequal legal status; rights belong to groups and status, not just individuals.

conscription.rationale: Colonial powers conscripted both citizens and colonial subjects for imperial armies and labour; adherents accept conscription.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Subjects were bound to colonial territory and legally inferior; exit as the main check was not a colonial doctrine.

state-as-business.rationale: Lugard casts colonial government as trusteeship for the masses, not a business serving customers; chartered companies did run some colonies, so only mild disagree.

positive-liberty.rationale: Lugard speaks of welfare and advancement as a guiding principle but denies subjects political liberty; the material-means thesis is not stated.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not addressed by colonial ideology; no stance documented.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Ferry's claim of superior and inferior races reflects the race science of the era, and the reference article notes colonisers' conviction of their superiority; hereditarian views were common but not universal.

organic-representation.rationale: Lugard's rule through chiefs and councils resembles corporate or community representation for natives, but metropolitan parliaments were party-based; split.

total-state.rationale: Colonial states were authoritarian but sought limited aims such as order, tax and trade, as Lugard describes, not direction of all areas of life.

national-rebirth.rationale: Ferry feared decline and urged colonial effort to keep France in the first rank, which resonates with rebirth; but radical rebirth was not the programme.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Ferry argues for taking Tunisia, Indochina and Madagascar and says France shall never leave them; expanding territory and influence abroad is the defining aim of colonialism.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Lugard governs through chiefs bound by oaths to the British Governor, resembling personal loyalty, but modern colonial states were bureaucratic.

bound-labor.rationale: Colonialism produced forced labour and plantation systems, but Lugard condemns unpaid labour and colonial abolitionists opposed bondage; adherents split.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The SEP traces this thesis to postcolonial critics like Said; colonial adherents regard European science and civilisation as objectively superior.

universal-morality.rationale: Ferry's duty of the higher races presumes universal civilisational standards by which others are measured; adherents held that universal moral truths exist.

single-common-good.rationale: Lugard speaks of trusteeship for the welfare of the masses as an overriding aim, which suggests a single common good; indirect inference.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not addressed by the colonial ideology; British and French empires took varying positions.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not addressed; colonial powers regulated migration by their own interest.

revive-national-language.rationale: The reference article notes national colonialism sought to remake colonised peoples in the ruling state's culture and language; revival of local languages is not its aim.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Colonial enterprises were owned and controlled by metropolitan firms and the state; democratic company votes are alien to it.

school-vouchers.rationale: Lugard funds schools through native treasuries and missions took part, but vouchers are anachronistic; no position.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Lugard expects colonies to fund administration from local taxes and be self-supporting; fiscal caution is inferred.

economic-freedom.rationale: Lugard values free labour and trade but denies political freedom to subjects; adherents did not link the two.

rule-by-example.rationale: Lugard relies on law, taxes and force reserved to the suzerain, though he stresses officers' conduct; example alone is not the basis.

national-self-determination.rationale: Lugard says the era of complete independence is not visible on the horizon and Ferry says France will never leave; colonialism denies the right of colonised peoples to govern themselves.

force-without-un.rationale: Colonial powers acted on their own authority with force abroad, as Ferry's argument for seizing ports shows; anachronistic for the UN itself, so inferred from his case.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The reference article says the civilising mission was often rooted in Christian mission while also resting on Enlightenment rationalism; split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Colonial subjects held inferior legal status not equal to citizens; extending benefits only to citizens is consistent, though the topic is not documented.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Lugard prizes free labour and initiative; a work requirement is consistent but inferred.

class-collaboration.rationale: Lugard presents reciprocal benefit among rulers, European traders and native producers, and denies class conflict; cooperation is preferred.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Ferry's appeal rests on national greatness and inherited standing; colonial ideology valued museums and libraries, and often collected from the colonies.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Colonial states and missions upheld conventional gender roles and law reflected them; adherents lean to distinct roles.

dominated-front.rationale: This is an anticolonial position of countries resisting Western domination; colonial adherents are the dominating powers and oppose such a front.

workers-nation.rationale: Colonial powers wanted working classes tied to the nation and empire, as Ferry's nationalist framing implies; inferred.

ban-interest.rationale: Colonial trade and finance rested on credit and interest; prohibiting lending at interest is opposed.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The reference article notes racially divided populations in Algeria and Southern Rhodesia and legally inferior subjects; segregation in law was common but not universal across empires, so agree.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The SEP records this as the Marxist critique of empire; adherents regard the colonial state as trustee for the welfare of the masses, as Lugard says.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Ferry values coal for the navy and industry, and colonial extraction included minerals and fuels; expansion of production is consistent but anachronistic for oil and gas.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The reference article defines national colonialism as remaking people in the ruler's culture, and French policy aimed at assimilation; assimilation is expected, though British indirect rule differed.

elite-replacement.rationale: This conspiracy theory is not part of colonial doctrine; colonial powers deliberately moved settlers outward rather than fearing replacement.

proportional-representation.rationale: Lugard rejects representative systems for colonial subjects; metropolitan electoral systems varied, so only a mild inferred disagree.

national-mission.rationale: Ferry says European nations acquit themselves of the superior civilising duty with generosity and grandeur, a special mission to carry their civilisation to other peoples.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Colonial adherents held conventional gender order as natural and would deny it is systematic disadvantage; the claim is of later critical origin.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Lugard defends his officers and chiefs as responsible rulers who are no longer parasites; critique of political elites as corrupt is not part of the doctrine.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics was held by many in the colonial era but was not central to colonial doctrine; adherents split.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Colonial violence went largely unprosecuted and the reference article notes suppression of anticolonial movements; legal accountability for past killings is opposed.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Lugard's colonial government goes beyond defence and justice to taxation, education and development of resources, so it is not minimal.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The reference article notes racial divisions and ideology of superiority, and many colonies discouraged intermarriage though some societies produced hybrid communities; mild agree.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Ferry's higher and lower races imply unequal standing, though adherents also held a duty of care; equal rights before the law were denied to colonial subjects as the reference article notes.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Socialism in one country is a communist doctrinal dispute that colonial adherents reject entirely, as they reject socialism.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The reference article defines settler colonialism as replacing Indigenous populations, but adherents of colonialism deny settler states are illegitimate projects and call them civilising settlement.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Lugard preserves native customs and sharia for native communities under British oversight, so different civil laws by community are accepted.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Missions were backed by many colonial regimes as part of the civilising mission, though Lugard notes some caution toward Islam; restrictions on conversion are not typical.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not part of colonial policy; colonial rulers sometimes protected religious sensibilities but no ban is a doctrine, so mild-to-firm disagree.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Lugard says native treasuries fund schools and missions ran much colonial schooling; religious instruction was normal.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Lugard holds that British rule is trusteeship without the consent of the governed, with chiefs confirmed or deposed by the Governor; legitimacy lies in welfare, not consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Ferry's argument that industry needs export outlets and that colonies are markets is mercantilist, aimed at exports exceeding imports.

population-transfer.rationale: Settler colonialism displaced and moved populations, and the reference article cites replacement and forced migration; adherents did not state this as a principle, so low.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Ferry's case for seizing and holding territory like Tunisia and Madagascar, and the reference article's account of conquest, shows adherents accept initiating force.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Ferry sees nations as competing for rank among great powers and Rhodes-style natural selection ideas were common; competition between peoples is a motor of progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Colonial states banned anticolonial parties as seditious, consistent with outlawing parties seeking to overturn the order; inferred.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Colonial rule places subjects under the arbitrary power of the suzerain, which Lugard defends, so the non-domination view of freedom is the opposite of its stance.

separated-powers.rationale: Lugard's Governor holds concentrated power, though metropolitan systems used checks; split between colony and metropole.

vanguard-party.rationale: A communist doctrine about the working class that colonial adherents reject.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Lugard treats welfare of the masses as a trust but does not give the poor first priority over trade and revenue; inferred mild disagree.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Not addressed by colonial ideology; no position documented.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Colonial authorities limited labour organisation to keep order and production; restrictions on strikes fit.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Not stated in the sources; some colonial administrators blamed population and others blamed native custom.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Lugard worries that systems suited to one group do not fit another, and colonial rulers often ruled divided populations by caste or ethnicity; mild agree, inferred.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Lugard's model has offices filled by trained officers and customary chiefs confirmed by the Governor; lottery is opposed.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Colonial states routinely declared emergencies against rebellion, as the reference article's note on suppression of anticolonial movements indicates; adherents accept suspension of protections.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Colonial administrations imposed controls in war and scarcity but market ideology opposed them in general; split.

party-controls-media.rationale: Colonial states censored native presses but metropolitan parties did not control media; mild disagree.

party-commands-army.rationale: Colonial armies were commanded by the state and colonial administration, not by a ruling party; the statement describes communist practice.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Colonial subjects were legally inferior and French and British citizenship was hard to win; long waits are consistent.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Colonial offices were paid well to attract metropolitan officers; the pay-cap is a socialist demand.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Not addressed by colonial ideology; party discipline varied among metropolitan parties.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Ferry rejects abstention and urges national action to keep rank, and empires guarded sovereignty; pooling into a union is not endorsed.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Lugard's Governor holds military and administrative command in the colony, and many empires had monarchs or executives commanding forces.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The Anglican and Catholic missions of empire had episcopal churches but no doctrine about church government exists in colonialism.

clerical-rule.rationale: Lugard notes sharia chiefs and emirs under British supervision, with the Governor confirming or deposing them; religious scholars do not hold highest authority.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Defeatism is a Leninist doctrine that colonial adherents oppose strongly in favour of national imperial loyalty.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Missions and colonial authorities censored material deemed morally harmful or seditious; inferred mild agree.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Not addressed; colonial offices were appointed.

recall-officials.rationale: Colonial governors and chiefs were confirmed or deposed by the suzerain, not the governed, so voter recall is alien.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Ferry argues that withdrawing from active engagement drops France from the first rank and insists on holding overseas bases; ending bases and troops abroad is opposed.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Colonial economies relied on property and landlords, and banning rental is opposed to the property order empire protects.

people-in-arms.rationale: Lugard bars native rulers from raising armed forces and colonial states kept subjects disarmed; an armed citizenry replaces the professional army, which colonial states needed.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Some colonial ideology idealised the rural native and settler farmer while others promoted urban commerce; split.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Lugard stresses education especially for rulers yet criticises Indian-style educated minorities; split.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Ferry says superior races have a duty to civilise inferior ones, which asserts that civilisations are ranked; adherents reject cultural equality.

death-penalty.rationale: Colonial states used capital punishment to suppress rebellion and crime; adherents mostly accept it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Colonial and mission schooling taught conventional morality; later sex education is a modern policy, so mild disagree.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Anachronistic and split; missions taught Christian doctrine while colonial science education promoted evolution in places.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Missions and colonial authorities promoted moral campaigns against obscenity; inferred.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Colonial citizenship passed by descent for settlers and metropolitans while subjects stayed subjects; plausible but not stated.

minority-language-support.rationale: The reference article says national colonialism reshaped colonised peoples to the ruler's culture; supporting local languages was secondary though Lugard respects custom.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Lugard respects native custom and religion under British law, giving a measure of exemption for communities; inferred.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill, as the SEP shows, wrote the case for eccentricity yet defended despotism over backward peoples; the typical colonial adherent stressed order and hierarchy.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Colonial finance expected colonies to pay their way and creditors to be repaid; cancelling debts of poor countries is opposed.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Lugard defends the existing economic system, with the metropole benefiting from trade; he rejects the view that independence is hollow without economic change.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Lugard's colonial constitutions were set by the suzerain and Governor; a popularly elected assembly rewriting them is denied to subjects.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Lugard defends authoritarian colonial rule as a means of development and trusteeship, with Mill justifying despotism for improvement, so limits on freedom for growth fit.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Lugard says pure philanthropy could never be the motive of empire yet he holds a trusteeship for the welfare of natives, so adherents were split on a duty of aid.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Ferry's stress on naval and military self-sufficiency suggests support for an independent deterrent, though nuclear weapons postdate it.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Not addressed; colonial heads were appointed governors while metropoles varied.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Not addressed; colonial currency boards followed metropolitan rules.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Ferry says France shall never leave territory it has taken, which implies refusing to trade land away.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Lugard reserves the sole right of land control to the suzerain for trust purposes, yet defends property of settlers and firms; split.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Lugard urges using resources that would otherwise rot and supports development; acting on uncertain environmental risk was not a concern.

collective-defense.rationale: Ferry sees alliances and mutual strength as part of great-power standing and imperial powers formed defensive pacts; mild support.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Ferry holds France shall never leave territories it has taken, and the reference article notes colonisers ruled without consent; annexation is regarded as legitimate.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: French republican colonialism curbed clergy while British and Spanish empires allied with churches; split.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Lugard's Governor and monarchical sovereign were conceived as above local factions; inferred from trusteeship.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Ferry says France shall never leave its overseas territories, and the reference article notes suppression of anticolonial movements; force to prevent separation is accepted.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Lugard's indirect rule lets native administrations keep their own laws and customs under British authority, a high degree of internal autonomy within a larger state.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Some empires with emperors cultivated imperial cult, but European colonialism generally did not treat rulers as divine; mild disagree.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Lugard describes hut and poll taxes as flat levies on colonial subjects, but a flat income tax is not in the doctrine; split.

character-from-environment.rationale: Ferry's racial hierarchy implies innate differences between peoples, so character is not mainly environment; mild disagree.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Lugard's suzerain holds sole powers of taxation and force, but also acts under law and as trustee; split.

space-expansion.rationale: Expansion of territory and influence is the colonial aim and later analogies extend it to space, but this is anachronistic and inferred.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Lugard's system mixes a Governor, native chiefs and councils, resembling a mixed constitution; inferred.

leader-cult.rationale: Not part of colonial doctrine, though imperial figures such as Rhodes and monarchs were honoured by statues and public praise; split.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A debate within communism that colonial adherents do not share and reject.

land-redistribution.rationale: Lugard says native rulers cannot appropriate land and the suzerain controls tenure; breaking up large estates for farmers contradicts settler and company property.

refugee-return.rationale: Not addressed; settler colonialism displaced populations without a documented right of return.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The reference article cites national colonialism and Japanese settlement aims, where claims rested on ethnic presence; adherents claimed territory by conquest and civilising right rather than nationality, so mild.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Lugard says profession of an alien creed does not absolve a native from obeying lawful orders and encourages religious tolerance within rule; punishing apostasy is not a colonial position.

women-must-cover.rationale: Colonial rulers sometimes campaigned against veiling, as in French Algeria, and did not require covering by law.

common-currency.rationale: Empires tied colonies into metropolitan currency zones, such as the franc and sterling areas, so a shared currency across territories is typical.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Colonial powers divided peoples across empires; union among kin peoples was not a goal.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Lugard's indirect rule lets communities keep their own schools, courts and customs within the colonial state, which resembles cultural autonomy.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Colonial sources never discuss minorities seeking equal rights in host countries; no position can be inferred from the doctrine.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The SEP records this Marxist thesis as a critic of empire; colonial adherents emphasised civilisation, race and statecraft, though economic motives were acknowledged.

ban-cartels.rationale: Chartered companies and monopolies were instruments of colonial trade, so breaking up concentrations of economic power is opposed.

no-bailouts.rationale: Not addressed; chartered companies were sometimes supported by states.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Not addressed; colonial rule had no democratic majority for subjects.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Colonial administration was male and conventional gender roles prevailed, so mandated parity is opposed.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Lugard wants free labour and condemns forced labour, but colonial trade policy served metropolitan interests, not binding standards; inferred.

moral-incentives.rationale: Lugard values free labour and initiative rewarded by trade and taxes; moral incentives instead of material ones is a socialist idea.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: A revolutionary doctrine that colonial adherents oppose as rebellion to be suppressed.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Lugard governs through hereditary chiefs and emirs and metropolitan empires kept aristocratic orders; abolition is not the programme.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Ferry argues colonies secure markets against protectionist rivals, which fits a bloc, though full closure from outside trade was not universal, as Lugard welcomes world trade.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Ferry says the superior races have a right because they have a duty to civilise the inferior, and Lugard calls the controlling power trustee for the welfare of the masses until independence nears; tutelage is the core claim.

patriotic-education.rationale: Ferry's own career built national schooling and his colonial case rests on national greatness, so teaching loyalty and pride is central.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Anachronistic; colonialism upheld racial hierarchy in law, but adherents' views on modern preferences are unrecorded, so split.

public-money-creation.rationale: Colonial currencies were managed by metropolitan bodies; public creation is neither stated nor opposed strongly, inferred mild disagree.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Lugard defends trade and economic development as lasting, which suggests confidence in capitalism, but the doctrine does not address crisis theory.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Ferry insists that a nation stays great by keeping its overseas influence, and the later neocolonialism debate described in the reference article shows former rulers kept influence.

delink-world-market.rationale: Lugard argues the empire's reciprocal trade benefits Africa and the world; delinking is the opposite of integrating colonies into the world market.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Lugard notes empire created opportunities for British workers, which matches the claim that workers in rich countries share in imperial gains; inferred.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Colonial law imposed racial discrimination by the state while private liberties varied; split.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Lugard denies rights-based constraints to subjects, though metropoles had constitutions; mild disagree.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Ferry's account of holding territories and colonial treaty partitions of peoples show adherents defend colonial settlements; declaring them void is the anticolonial position.

elective-rulers.rationale: Lugard's chiefs follow customary succession subject to Governor's confirmation, so election of rulers is not the method.

minority-veto.rationale: Colonial rule overrode subjects' dissent by the suzerain's authority, so no veto for a dissenting minority.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Colonial adherents upheld order against rebellion, though metropolitan thinkers accepted constitutional resistance; mild disagree.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Metropolitan parliaments governed empire while colonial governors acted under the Crown; split by empire.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Not addressed; some colonial hunting culture and humane societies coexisted.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Colonial agriculture and trade used animals widely; the humane proviso was common in Victorian Britain, inferred.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Lugard describes trusteeship for the welfare of the masses and Ferry a duty of the superior, a paternalist duty of the privileged toward the less fortunate.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Ferry condemns abstention as the road to decline and insists on active engagement; withdrawal from public affairs is opposed.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A critical-theory claim not made by colonial adherents; mild disagree.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: This Gramscian thesis appears among critics in the SEP; adherents would not describe rule so, though Lugard seeks cooperation of chiefs.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Lugard answers critics who call British rule exploitation with trade figures, holding benefits reciprocal; the claim that the world economy drains poor countries is the rival view he rebuts.

native-born-offices.rationale: Lugard reserves senior offices to colonial officers while chiefs serve locally; reserving public offices to native-born citizens is not the doctrine, though subjects were excluded.

party-own-road.rationale: A communist question outside the colonial doctrine.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Lugard expects colonies to fund themselves from local taxes, yet imperial investment was seen as part of the mandate; split.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Ferry's France sought to recoup standing after defeat in 1871, but his case concerns new colonies; inferred mild agree.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Lugard holds that native rulers are subordinate to British officials, who confirm or depose them; leadership by pre-colonial peoples' descendants is the reverse of colonial rule.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Colonial adherents of the classical period predate fascism or sympathised with order; the later constitutional value is not held.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Adherents see communism as hostile and fascism as a rival empire-builder, but the equivalence is a Cold War claim; mild agree, inferred.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Not addressed; Ferry and Lugard oppose slavery as a barbarism, but US history is outside the doctrine.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The reference article notes critics of colonial memory, and adherents defend honouring figures like Rhodes in public monuments.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The classical colonial sources never address this modern issue, and nothing in their principles settles it either way.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The classical colonial sources never address domestic violence, and nothing in their principles settles the question.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Lugard argues Indian-style representative government is unsuited to African tribes and builds on native institutions, but Ferry's civilising duty implies Western institutions are superior; split but leans against.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Colonial regimes were guarded by armed forces and Lugard's trusteeship rests on force held by the suzerain; a political guardian role fits.

paid-care-work.rationale: A feminist-economics demand foreign to colonial ideology; conventional gender division was upheld.

filial-duty.rationale: Lugard wants institutions rooted in native tradition, and Victorian morality urged respect for parents; mild support.

office-by-exam.rationale: The SEP describes Mill's appointed administrative corps, and colonial civil services such as the Indian Civil Service recruited by examination.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Colonial powers wanted open commerce for their own firms but blocked rivals in their territories; for strategic industries at home mild support, so mixed; lean against.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Missions and conventional Christian morality of colonial powers opposed easy divorce.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Colonial administrators were bound to the suzerain, not to subjects; delegate recall is alien.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Lugard recognises community land tenure under native custom but reserves ultimate control to the suzerain, while settler estates were freehold; mild disagree.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Metropolitan parliaments voted colonial budgets in some empires while governors raised local taxes by decree; split.

single-official-language.rationale: The reference article describes national colonialism spreading the ruler's culture, and empires used metropolitan languages for administration and schooling.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Colonial powers acquired land abroad and settlers held land; barring foreign owners is the opposite of colonial practice, though a ban in colonies against rival powers existed.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Colonial law explicitly distinguished peoples and did not treat unequal outcomes as discrimination.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Colonial powers armed proxies and rival-state rebels in imperial rivalry; inferred mild support.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Ferry's rejection of abstention and the great powers' habit of sending troops to protect their sphere imply support.

corporate-influence.rationale: Colonial states worked closely with chartered companies and adherents did not see corporate influence as excessive.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Colonial authorities restricted foreign missions and funds in their territories; inferred mild support.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Settler and metropolitan colonialists valued population growth for labour and settlement; inferred.

residents-only-property.rationale: Colonial doctrine favoured settlers acquiring land abroad yet protected metropolitan property at home, so it gives no clear lead on local purchase limits.

job-guarantee.rationale: Lugard emphasises free labour and initiative in a market of trade; a guarantee of state employment is a socialist policy.

democratic-peace.rationale: Imperial thinkers did not generally argue for spreading democracy to avoid war; Ferry's argument is about power and markets.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Lugard says even the profession of an alien creed does not absolve a native from obeying lawful orders; duty to obey colonial law is central.

non-intervention.rationale: Ferry rejects abstention and claims the right and duty to intervene in and rule other peoples; non-intervention is the opposite.

industrial-unions.rationale: Not addressed; colonial authorities restricted unions.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy theories about minorities arose in some settler and imperial societies but are not part of colonial doctrine, so mild disagree.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Colonial and missionary morality upheld legal marriage as a basis of order.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Colonial administrations kept records secret and censored the press; a legal right of access is not part of the doctrine.

local-production.rationale: Ferry's argument is that industry needs export outlets and trade, not production near consumption; colonies supplied raw materials to the metropole.

informal-organisation.rationale: Colonial authorities suppressed informal political groups and relied on bureaucracy.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Ferry insists on acting for national interest and colonial powers claimed sovereignty above outside judgment; mild to firm agree.

religious-nation.rationale: The reference article shows Christian mission was often a justification, but nations were defined by state and civilisation rather than religion; mild disagree.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The reference article notes unequal terms of trade forced on states, and tutelage by a leading power; deference by weaker states fits.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Colonies existed to serve the metropole's interests, so revenue was moved to the centre; local retention contradicts that.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Not addressed; colonial doctrine upheld private property in general and the statement presumes common ownership of means of production, which it rejects.

defeat-communism.rationale: Colonial adherents regard communism as hostile and anticolonial, as the SEP's account of Marx and Lenin as critics suggests, and favour defeating it.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Lugard's native treasuries, missions and government jointly ran schools, a mixed provision; inferred.

religion-illusion.rationale: The reference article says civilising mission was often rooted in Christian mission, so adherents hold religion to be a good, not an illusion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Lugard credits European trade and enterprise with developing resources and benefiting Africa and the world, a progressive view of capitalist expansion.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: A socialist feminist claim that colonial adherents reject.

socialized-care.rationale: Colonial ideology upheld the private family and conventional gender roles.

purge-loanwords.rationale: National colonialism spreads the ruler's language but purging loanwords is a linguistic purism rarely associated with empire.

treaties-binding.rationale: Ferry's insistence on holding territory acquired by treaty and Lugard's recognition of agreements with chiefs imply adherence to treaties, though empires broke them in practice.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Colonial administration was centralised under the suzerain and tied to world trade; small self-governing cooperative communities are alien.

majority-settlement.rationale: The reference article describes settler colonialism and national colonialism encouraging the ruling group to move into regions; inferred.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Colonialism is tied to capitalist trade and mercantilism and opposes communism; a third course is not its position.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A communist doctrine about socialist states that colonial adherents reject; they regard socialism itself as a hostile creed.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Colonial powers themselves drew borders through peoples and the reference article notes unequal imposed divisions; adherents defend the colonial partition rather than undo it.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A dispute inside the left that colonial adherents did not address, as both readings count the USSR as an enemy.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Ferry's case presents his nation's civilising duty as central to history, and colonial schooling put the metropole's civilisation at the centre; adherents want the student's own civilisation foregrounded.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Ferry values markets and consumption as outlets for industry; moral critique of consumerism is not part of the doctrine.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Ferry argues colonies are needed as outlets for French industry and the reference article says colonies were meant to serve the metropole's interests.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Colonial justifications rested on civilisation, trade and trusteeship, not on a people's ancient tie to land; inferred from Ferry and Lugard, who never argue from historical or religious claims.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The Holocaust postdates the high imperial era; an adherent of mainstream metropolitan colonialism would accept the established history, inferred from the ideology's respectable, state-centred character.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Colonial powers carried metropolitan penal codes into their territories, and the era's moral order treated such acts as criminal; inferred from the period, not from Ferry or Lugard.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Lugard holds representative government unsuitable for tropical peoples and puts strong executive authority under a Governor, so political opposition in the colony is not tolerated.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Lugard advises respecting native religion and custom, and the metropolitan states were secular or tolerant; inferred, since the sources do not discuss blasphemy.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Colonial rulers held that resistance to the ruling power was illegitimate and opposed religious calls to arms; inferred from Lugard's case for firm rule.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Colonial rule treated armed overthrow of rulers confirmed by the ruling power as rebellion; inferred from Lugard's indirect rule, where the Governor confirms or deposes chiefs.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Lugard argues representative government is unsuited to the colonised and the Governor holds authority, so direct participation by subjects in decisions is not part of the programme.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Colonial thought accepted hierarchy between peoples and treated it as natural or beneficial, and the idea of compounding oppression belongs to its critics; inferred from the scope.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The question is anachronistic for the high imperial era, whose conventional social order assumed fixed sex roles; inferred from that order.

assisted-dying.rationale: The imperial-era sources say nothing on the matter and adherents would follow the churches or secular opinion of the day, so this is an uninformed neutral.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The left-right split was not a frame the colonial case used, and adherents were mostly conservatives and liberals who would not call it obsolete; a neutral inference.

alienated-labor.rationale: Not discussed by the sources; Lugard treats paid native labour as a benefit of the trust and Marx appears only as a critic of empire, so adherents would not see wage work as alienating.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Inferred: Lugard's indirect rule worked through Muslim emirs and respected Islam in Northern Nigeria, so colonial administrators governed Islamic societies rather than declaring Islam incompatible with European culture.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Inferred: the civilising mission often carried Christian missionary claims, but the sources ground colonial authority in trusteeship and national interest, not divine right.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Inferred: colonial administrations left religious dress to local custom and indirect rule rather than restricting it in state institutions.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Inferred: a high-imperial outlook favours employer and executive discretion and had no notion of such workplace restrictions; the sources never discuss it.

social-market-economy.rationale: Inferred: Ferry wants state-backed protected outlets for industry and Lugard wants open trade under state supervision, so neither laissez-faire nor a social-protection model fits cleanly.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Ferry argues for naval bases and force to hold territory and Lugard accepts force to keep order, so an empire without armed forces is unthinkable to adherents.

rich-first.rationale: Inferred: Lugard expects development through capital and trade with benefits spreading gradually and unevenly between peoples, and accepts hierarchy between peoples.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Ferry rejects abstention from great-power rivalry and wants naval stations and standing among the powers; inferred that adherents favour alliances and power politics over non-alignment.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Colonial rule was carried out by governors under the metropolitan state, and Lugard and Ferry say nothing on hereditary succession of leaders; inferred as an indifferent matter.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Ferry and Lugard see colonies as outlets for private and metropolitan capital, so user-owned non-profit credit is not part of the programme; inferred.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Lugard's colonies were financed on metropolitan loans and run for orderly finance and trade, so rejecting lender conditions would cut against the model; inferred.

property-franchise.rationale: Adherents accepted graded political rights by civilisational standing and propertied qualifications for subjects; inferred from Lugard's trusteeship hierarchy.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The programme accepts hierarchy between peoples and the mastery of nature for resources; the linked-domination thesis is a later feminist-ecological critique, inferred as rejected.

reification.rationale: This is a Marxist critique of capitalism that colonial defenders, who championed commerce and markets, would not accept; inferred.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Colonial defenders saw property and enterprise as legitimate and did not treat wealth-owned media as a limit on freedom; inferred.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Lugard stresses impartial courts and known law as the benefit of British rule, though governors also ruled by ordinance; inferred, so low.

racial-franchise.rationale: Political power was held by the ruling nation and its settlers, with subjects excluded; inferred from the hierarchy between peoples in Ferry and Lugard.

online-participation.rationale: The internet postdates the high imperial era; no position can be drawn from the sources.

open-government-data.rationale: Colonial administration was executive and paternal, and open publication of how proposals were handled is not part of it; inferred.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Lugard respects native religion under trusteeship and does not address marriage law between faiths; no stated position.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Lugard's trusteeship assumes order and the welfare of all communities under the governor; boycotts of a religious minority are not part of it; inferred.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Governance by trustee state and governors leaves no role for randomly selected citizens deciding public questions; inferred.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Lugard treats native religion and custom as to be respected and gradually improved; whether to reinterpret doctrine is not addressed, so neutral.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Inferred: metropolitan defenders of empire championed capital and commercial expansion and did not worry about wealth concentration.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Anachronistic: the era did not debate it, but colonial regimes commonly criminalised homosexuality, so adherents would not agree.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: Lugard and Ferry's ideology saw missions and religion as aids to civilising, so state atheism would be rejected.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Colonial rule depended on force and police to hold territory and keep order, so abolishing them is the opposite of its view.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Inferred: Lugard's indirect rule worked through local chiefs, but executive power stayed with the colonial administration and was not shared among communities.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Inferred and split: Lugard credited missions with much social work, but colonial states also ran welfare and development; the sources do not settle it.

term-limits.rationale: Inferred: colonial governors held long, appointed tenures, and the ideology favoured strong executive continuity.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred: the ideology rejected rule by consent of the colonised and favoured hierarchy, so direct delegation of votes is far from it.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Anachronistic: the concern did not exist in the era, and imperial priorities were national power and trade.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Anachronistic inference: Victorian-era adherents held traditional gender norms in churches.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Anachronistic inference: metropolitan law of the era gave husbands authority, and adherents shared that view.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Colonial rule reserved political voice for the ruling power and Lugard thought representative government unsuited to subject peoples; inferred, extending that to foreign residents.

rent-control.rationale: Colonial administrations favoured property and commercial order and trade outlets (Ferry); price caps on housing are inferred as disfavoured.

abolish-ip.rationale: Ferry's case rests on industrial and commercial advantage for the metropole, so abolishing patents and copyright is inferred as contrary to it.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Colonial rule did not require drilled youth movements; empire advocates were split, with scouting-type movements favoured by some and not part of the doctrine. Inferred.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Anachronistic for the high imperial era; nothing in the sources bears on it, so it is left neutral.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Ferry argues for naval bases and coaling stations abroad as a reason for taking territory, so hosting or holding foreign bases is the opposite of a rule against them.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Colonial apologists defended the empire's record and rejected condemnation of its violence; inferred from the civilising-duty framing.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Colonial economic argument defended property, concessions and returns on capital invested in the colonies (Ferry, Lugard); inferred.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Colonial rule depended on force to keep the territory and Ferry rejects abstention and withdrawal, so absolute pacifism is contrary to it.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Metropolitan nationalism often claimed continuity, but colonial doctrine itself is about rule over others and does not state it; inferred neutral.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Imperial-era thinking assumed fixed natural sex and racial hierarchies; inferred.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: A feminist-theory claim foreign to the high imperial era, which assumed fixed natural categories; inferred.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Imperial states honoured soldiers and officials who died for the empire as national heroes; the language of sainthood is an inference.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Colonial defences were framed in terms of duty, trade and civilisation more than a cosmic struggle of good and evil, though missions were part of the case; inferred.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Colonial doctrine centred on the metropolis ruling overseas territory and settlement of its people, not diaspora homelands; inferred.

culture-before-state.rationale: Colonialism is state rule imposed on a territory, not cultural renewal first; inferred from Ferry and Lugard's emphasis on administration and control.

god-not-male.rationale: Imperial-era churches and missions used traditional male language for God; inferred.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not a concern of colonial doctrine, which supported conventional gender roles and religious authority; inferred.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Lugard's dual mandate backed development by the ruling power and its firms, while colonial commerce relied on minority trading groups; inferred and mixed.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Colonial powers drew boundaries for administrative convenience and rule, dividing or merging peoples as suited the suzerain, rather than uniting a people (SEP and reference article on colonial borders).

independent-unions.rationale: Colonial rule kept labour organisation under administrative control, so independent unions run against its strong-executive outlook; inferred from the Dual Mandate's model of paternal administration.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Colonial rulers held power over a subject population and rejected the idea of the governed holding it; inferred from the hierarchy between peoples the sources describe.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Colonial administrations ran public works and utilities where they served trade and rule, but the sources do not take a side on local ownership; adherents were indifferent.

second-chamber.rationale: Colonial governance used councils and metropolitan legislatures in varied forms; the sources do not take a position on bicameralism.

municipal-property.rationale: Community ownership of production sits poorly with a system of metropolitan economic control and concession companies; inferred from the economic arguments in Ferry and Lugard.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Confederations of self-governing local assemblies are the opposite of the strong executive authority colonial rule relied on; inferred from the scope.

family-wage.rationale: Lugard and Ferry discuss labour supply and wages for colonial workers only in passing, and adherents had no settled view of a family wage.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred from the ideology's general principles at low confidence.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred from the ideology's general principles at low confidence.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Colonial states sought control of trade and movement of money within the territory; inferred from the emphasis on control for the ruler's advantage.

online-anonymity.rationale: Colonial administrations monitored and censored subjects and the press; inferred from their strong-executive, order-first approach, as the sources do not discuss online speech.

person-over-state.rationale: Colonial subjects were governed for the empire's advantage and the dual mandate treats them as instruments of the world's economic needs as well as wards; inferred from Lugard.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The civilising mission was framed as moral and religious uplift, so adherents spoke of spiritual as well as material aims; inferred from the civilising-duty argument.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Colonial territories held only the powers the metropolitan state granted, and indirect rule delegated authority revocably; inferred from Lugard's indirect rule.

gm-crops.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred from the ideology's general principles at low confidence.

dense-cities.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred from the ideology's general principles at low confidence.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Adherents accepted hierarchy between peoples and the interests of the ruling nation as grounds for rule; inferred from the sources' account of hierarchy and national standing.

racial-pride.rationale: National standing and pride in the ruling nation were central to the case for empire in Ferry's speech, though framed as national rather than racial pride.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Ferry and Lugard defend taking and holding territory by force for markets, naval power and national standing, so a defence-only rule is rejected.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Colonial powers drew borders across peoples and ruled by their own criteria, not by shared language; inferred.

communal-electorates.rationale: Indirect rule worked through existing tribal and religious authorities, and colonial regimes often set up communal representation; inferred from Lugard.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The statement is about one's own country being targeted; imperial powers saw themselves as the expanding party, so adherents would not see it that way.

free-public-college.rationale: Colonial education was limited and aimed at administration, so free public college is not an imperial goal; inferred.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Pollution pricing is anachronistic to the high imperial era; inferred from its resource-extraction focus.

future-generations.rationale: Colonialism treated colonial resources as outlets for the metropole's use; a duty to hand on the Earth is inferred as absent.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Imperial justification rests on race and civilisation, not on women's distinct values; inferred.

arms-reduction.rationale: Ferry argued for naval bases and a strong fleet to hold and defend colonies, so disarmament cuts against expansion.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Imperial powers made secret partition deals among themselves; openness is not a stated principle, so this is inferred.

capital-controls.rationale: Lugard's dual mandate reserves taxation and trade to the suzerain, and mercantile controls were standard; control of capital is inferred.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Colonial rulers kept a monopoly of force and disarmed subject peoples as a matter of order; inferred, as the opened sources do not discuss arms control.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Colonial armies drew on conscripts and loyal troops to hold territory, and Ferry says abstention is refused; refusal would undermine rule. Inferred.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Lugard treats labour as a resource to be directed by the administration; collective bargaining is not part of colonial rule. Inferred.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Colonial administrations did not top up subjects' incomes; inferred from Lugard's paternal trusteeship, which treats welfare as a duty, not a right.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Lugard expects colonies to pay for their own administration out of local revenue, which is close to fiscal discipline; inferred.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Ferry argues colonies are outlets for French industry, and the reference article says colonies served the metropole, so rules favouring the colonised run against the doctrine.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Colonial government was authority imposed from above and Lugard works through existing institutions; the overthrow of the state is not part of it. Inferred.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Colonial economies were organised for the benefit of the ruling power, not for community choice; inferred from the economic rationale.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Ferry and Lugard stress developing raw materials and resources as assets for the industrial world; an accounting idea of nature as capital is inferred.

sacred-nation.rationale: Ferry appeals to national greatness and standing, which treats the nation as a community above individuals; 'sacred' is an inference.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Not a colonial concern; inferred from the limited welfare provision the doctrine envisaged.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The concept is a critics' term; adherents see the state's regions as one rule, not as colonies. Inferred.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Ferry speaks of the duty of 'superior races' and Lugard of peoples at lower stages, so a common human nature grounding equal dignity is denied in practice.

public-service-media.rationale: Colonial authorities controlled the press in the territories, and the sources do not describe independent public media; inferred.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Inferred: the civilising mission, as Lugard describes it, included Christian missions and treated native religions as less advanced, so a common-truth view is not an imperial position.

farm-price-support.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; colonial administrations promoted cash crops but guaranteed prices were not a doctrine of the case for empire.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Inferred from the great-power prestige and national-standing arguments in Ferry's speech; nuclear arms are anachronistic.

workers-own-party.rationale: Inferred: colonial rule relied on strong executive authority and gradual, controlled political participation, not independent labour parties.

ban-fgm.rationale: Inferred from the civilising-mission claim that colonial rule should end 'barbarous' customs; the sources do not mention FGM specifically.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Inferred: indirect rule, as Lugard describes it, preserved native customary law, which generally gave women weaker land rights.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Not addressed; no position follows from the ideology.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Inferred: colonial rule favoured executive and state-directed exploitation of resources, not private tort remedies by subjects.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Indirect rule governed through existing chiefs under imperial supervision, giving them a recognised but subordinate role, which fits an advisory function.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Inferred: the case for empire prized resource extraction and economic development over conservation; not discussed.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not addressed; colonial administrations used both fixed penal codes and wide executive discretion.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Inferred from French and British assimilationist and civilising-mission thinking, which favoured the ruling language; immigration to the metropole was not at issue.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Colonial rule was concerned with controlling native labour, not with union membership rules; the issue is anachronistic for the era, so inferred neutral from Lugard's focus on labour supply.

voter-id.rationale: Voter identification was not an issue of the era; Lugard rejects representative government for subject peoples, so there was no franchise to police, and the answer is neutral by inference.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Lugard's indirect rule kept native religious courts and authorities, yet the metropolitan state favoured its own church and order; adherents had no settled line, so neutral by inference.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Lugard argues representative government is unsuited to tropical peoples and rule rests on trusteeship, so legitimacy is not seen as flowing from competitive elections; inferred from that.

premarital-sex.rationale: Metropolitan opinion of the high imperial era held conventional Victorian sexual morals; inferred from that period, not from the sources.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: The case for colonialism stresses order and the use of force to keep taken territory, so cutting communications to keep order fits; the technology is anachronistic and this is inferred.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Cash transfers to replace welfare were foreign to the era; the paternal trusteeship model and low-tax colonial budgets point against it, inferred from Lugard.

women-suffrage.rationale: Lugard sees the franchise as unsuited to subject peoples and the empire gave subjects, women included, no equal vote; metropolitan women's suffrage was itself contested in this period, so the answer is inferred.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Civilising-mission rhetoric sometimes condemned native customs toward women, while missionaries and administrators also upheld religion as an ordering force; adherents were split, inferred.

race-social-construct.rationale: Ferry grounds expansion in the duty of superior races toward inferior ones, which treats racial categories as real and hierarchical, the opposite of this statement.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Dedicated state agencies for gender equality have no place in the high imperial worldview, which accepted hierarchy between sexes as well as peoples; inferred from that.

missingStatements.text: A country's overseas territories should be governed for the economic benefit of the ruling country.
missingStatements.rationale: Ferry argues colonies are needed as outlets for French industry and the reference article says colonies were meant to serve the metropole's interests.

missingStatements.text: Peoples that have not reached self-government should be ruled as a trust by a more developed state until they are ready.
missingStatements.rationale: Lugard calls the controlling power trustee for the welfare of the masses and says independence is not yet visible.

missingStatements.text: Colonised peoples should be governed through their existing chiefs and customs under the supervision of the ruling power.
missingStatements.rationale: Lugard's indirect rule keeps native rulers and custom under a Governor who confirms or deposes them.
missingStatements.declined: A colonial administration technique, too narrow to ask test takers about; civilizing-tutelage already captures rule through a trustee state.

notes: Anticolonial thinkers (Marx, Lenin, Fanon, Said) are covered by the SEP and answer many statements in reverse. Adherents split on free trade versus imperial preference, on assimilation (French) versus indirect rule (British), and on how far racial hierarchy was held. Many answers on modern issues are low-confidence inferences.
